front_blocks.md: Describe the **alpha-particle scattering experiment**.

back_blocks.md: The **alpha-particle scattering experiment** was Rutherford's experiment in which alpha particles were fired at thin gold foil, with a detector recording the deflection of particles at various angles, used to determine the structure of the atom.

cards.front_md: Describe the **alpha-particle scattering experiment**.
cards.back_md: The **alpha-particle scattering experiment** was Rutherford's experiment in which alpha particles were fired at thin gold foil, with a detector recording the deflection of particles at various angles, used to determine the structure of the atom.

front_blocks.md: What did the observation that most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil suggest?

back_blocks.md: It suggested that the atom is mainly **empty space**.

cards.front_md: What did the observation that most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil suggest?
cards.back_md: It suggested that the atom is mainly **empty space**.

front_blocks.md: What did the observation that some alpha particles deflected through small angles (less than 10°) suggest?

back_blocks.md: It suggested there is a **positive nucleus** at the centre of the atom, since two positive charges repel.

cards.front_md: What did the observation that some alpha particles deflected through small angles (less than 10°) suggest?
cards.back_md: It suggested there is a **positive nucleus** at the centre of the atom, since two positive charges repel.

front_blocks.md: What did the observation that a small number of alpha particles deflected straight back at angles greater than 90° suggest?

back_blocks.md: It suggested the **nucleus** is extremely **small**, and that the mass and charge of the atom are concentrated there.

cards.front_md: What did the observation that a small number of alpha particles deflected straight back at angles greater than 90° suggest?
cards.back_md: It suggested the **nucleus** is extremely **small**, and that the mass and charge of the atom are concentrated there.

front_blocks.md: In the alpha-particle scattering experiment, alpha particles were fired at a thin **..........** foil.

back_blocks.md: In the alpha-particle scattering experiment, alpha particles were fired at a thin **gold** foil.

cards.front_md: In the alpha-particle scattering experiment, alpha particles were fired at a thin **..........** foil.
cards.back_md: In the alpha-particle scattering experiment, alpha particles were fired at a thin **gold** foil.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The alpha-particle scattering experiment showed that the positive charge of an atom is spread evenly throughout its volume.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
The experiment showed that the positive charge is concentrated in a small, dense **nucleus**, not spread evenly (which the earlier 'plum pudding' model had assumed).

cards.front_md:

front_blocks.md: According to the conclusions of the alpha-particle scattering experiment, roughly how much larger is an atom than its nucleus?

back_blocks.md: Roughly **100,000 times** larger.

cards.front_md: According to the conclusions of the alpha-particle scattering experiment, roughly how much larger is an atom than its nucleus?

front_blocks.md: Define an **antimatter particle**.

back_blocks.md: An **antimatter particle** is identical to its matter counterpart but with the opposite charge.

cards.front_md: Define an **antimatter particle**.
cards.back_md: An **antimatter particle** is identical to its matter counterpart but with the opposite charge.

front_blocks.md: What is the antimatter counterpart of a **proton**, and what is its charge?

back_blocks.md: The **anti-proton**, with a charge of **-1**.

cards.front_md: What is the antimatter counterpart of a **proton**, and what is its charge?
cards.back_md: The **anti-proton**, with a charge of **-1**.

front_blocks.md: The atomic mass unit (*u*) is approximately equal to the mass of what?

back_blocks.md: The mass of one **proton** or **neutron**.

cards.front_md: The atomic mass unit (*u*) is approximately equal to the mass of what?
cards.back_md: The mass of one **proton** or **neutron**.

front_blocks.md: One atomic mass unit (*u*) is defined as 1/12 of the mass of a **..........** atom.

back_blocks.md: One atomic mass unit (*u*) is defined as 1/12 of the mass of a **carbon-12** atom.

cards.front_md: One atomic mass unit (*u*) is defined as 1/12 of the mass of a **..........** atom.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Most of the mass of an atom is due to its electrons.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Electrons have negligible mass (about 1/2000 of a proton or neutron); most of an atom's mass comes from the **protons** and **neutrons** in the nucleus.

front_blocks.md: Define the **nucleon number** (mass number).

back_blocks.md: The **nucleon number** is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.

cards.front_md: Define the **nucleon number** (mass number).

front_blocks.md: Define the **proton number** (atomic number).

back_blocks.md: The **proton number** is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom. In a neutral atom, it is also equal to the number of electrons.

cards.front_md: Define the **proton number** (atomic number).

front_blocks.md: How do you calculate the number of neutrons in an atom, given its nucleon number and proton number?

back_blocks.md: Number of neutrons = nucleon number (*A*) − proton number (*Z*)

cards.front_md: How do you calculate the number of neutrons in an atom, given its nucleon number and proton number?
cards.back_md: Number of neutrons = nucleon number (*A*) − proton number (*Z*)

front_blocks.md: Define an **isotope**.

back_blocks.md: An **isotope** is an atom (of the same element) that has an equal number of protons but a different number of neutrons.

cards.front_md: Define an **isotope**.
cards.back_md: An **isotope** is an atom (of the same element) that has an equal number of protons but a different number of neutrons.

front_blocks.md: Why are isotopes generally unstable?

back_blocks.md: Because they have an imbalance of neutrons and protons, so they constantly decay and emit radiation to reach a more stable form.

cards.front_md: Why are isotopes generally unstable?

Isotopes of an element have a different number of protons.

front_blocks.md: Define an **alpha (α) particle**.

back_blocks.md: An **alpha particle** is a high energy particle made up of 2 protons and 2 neutrons (the same as a helium nucleus), usually emitted from nuclei that are too large.

cards.front_md: Define an **alpha (α) particle**.
cards.back_md: An **alpha particle** is a high energy particle made up of 2 protons and 2 neutrons (the same as a helium nucleus), usually emitted from nuclei that are too large.

front_blocks.md: Why are alpha particles strongly ionising but weakly penetrating?

back_blocks.md: Alpha particles have a large charge (+2*e*), so they interact strongly with matter (highly ionising). This means they lose energy quickly and cannot travel far, so they are weakly penetrating and can be blocked by skin or a sheet of paper.

cards.front_md: Why are alpha particles strongly ionising but weakly penetrating?

front_blocks.md: What is the difference between a β⁻ particle and a β⁺ particle?

back_blocks.md: A **β⁻ particle** is a high energy electron, emitted by nuclei with too many neutrons.
A **β⁺ particle** is a high energy positron, emitted by nuclei with too many protons.

cards.front_md: What is the difference between a β⁻ particle and a β⁺ particle?

A **β⁺ particle** is a high energy positron, emitted by nuclei with too many protons.

front_blocks.md: Define a **gamma (γ) ray**.

back_blocks.md: A **gamma ray** is a high energy electromagnetic wave, emitted by a nucleus that needs to lose energy.

Gamma rays are the most ionising type of radiation.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
**Alpha** particles are the most strongly ionising, due to their large +2*e* charge; gamma rays are the least ionising of the three.

back_blocks.md: An **electron neutrino** is a subatomic particle with no charge and negligible mass, emitted from the nucleus (produced during β+ decay).

A neutrino carries an electric charge.

Electron neutrinos (and antineutrinos) are **uncharged**, with negligible mass.

front_blocks.md: Why do beta particles have a continuous range of kinetic energies, unlike alpha particles which have discrete energies?

back_blocks.md: The energy released in beta decay is **shared** between the beta particle and the neutrino (or antineutrino) in varying proportions, giving a continuous range of energies.
